Where it is plucked decides which modes are excited most: near the bridge, many harmonics and a bright sound; in the middle, few and a sweet sound. A mode that has a node exactly where it is plucked does not sound.

La flauta es un tubo abierto por los dos:
The flute is a tube open at both ends: it has all the harmonics, like the string. The clarinet behaves as a tube closed at the mouthpiece end, and in such a tube a quarter of a wavelength has to fit, three quarters, five quarters…: only the odd harmonics. It is exactly the spectrum of the previous topic's square wave, and that is why the square wave sounds like a clarinet.

And a closed tube sounds an octave lower than an open one of the same length: $\frac{v}{4L}$ against $\frac{v}{2L}$. That is why the stopped pipes of an organ give low notes with half the wood.
La frecuencia va con la <em>raíz</em> de: The frequency goes with the square root of the tension: $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$.
La fundamental está bien, pero el segund: The fundamental is right, but the second mode of a closed tube is not the double: it is the triple. The even harmonics do not exist in it.

The first line is the whole topic: the possible frequencies are whole multiples of $f_1 = \frac{v}{2L}$. That is the reason a string produces harmonics and not any old mixture: the geometry of the fixed ends leaves no other option.

The second says what the speed depends on: the tension $T$ (newtons) and the linear density $\mu$ (kilograms per metre). Tighter string, faster wave, higher note; thicker string, slower, lower. And the square root matters: to double the frequency you have to quadruple the tension, not double it.

Pitágoras estudió la cuerda con un monoc: Pythagoras studied the string with a monochord and found that the consonances were ratios of lengths. Mersenne measured in 1636 how the frequency depends on the length, the tension and the thickness: his three laws are the formula $f = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}$ shared out into three sentences. Brook Taylor, of the polynomials, computed the fundamental in 1713, and Jean le Rond d'Alembert wrote in 1747 the wave equation, the first partial differential equation in history, whose general solution is precisely two waves travelling in opposite directions. Daniel Bernoulli proposed that the solution was a sum of modes, and Euler did not believe him: it was the first version of the argument Fourier would settle half a century later.

It reads: “sine of k x minus omega t, plus sine of k x plus omega t, is two times sine of k x times cosine of omega t”.

It is the identity for the sum of sines as a product, and what it says is astonishing: the result no longer has $x$ and $t$ mixed together. Its shape in space is $\sin(kx)$, always the same, and all time does is multiply it by $\cos(\omega t)$: the curve swells and shrinks without moving along. That is why it is called standing. There are points that never move, where $\sin(kx) = 0$, the nodes, and points that oscillate at the maximum, the antinodes.
